title: Biobehavioral Mechanisms of Activity and Loss of Control Eating in Children
text:
Loss of control eating (LOCE) among children confers increased risk for eating disorders and other mental and
physical health consequences, yet little is known regarding mechanisms that contribute to LOCE across time
and at the momentary level. Physical activity and self-regulation are important modifiable behaviors that may
impact pediatric LOCE. The proposed research will examine biobehavioral mechanisms that link physical activity,
self-regulation, LOCE and related eating disorder psychopathology from late childhood to adolescence, with the
goal of informing future prevention and intervention efforts.

title: Mechanisms of Developmental Myelination
text:
Precisely controlled formation of myelin on central nervous system axons is essential for motor and intellectual
function. The long-term goal of this project is to understand how oligodendrocytes, which are glial cells of the
central nervous system, form specific amounts of myelin on select axons during development. Completion of
the project aims will substantially extend our understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which
myelin membrane is produced and modified by brain activity.

title: MODULATION OF CD5 SIGNALING TO ENHANCE ADOPTIVE T-CELL THERAPIES FOR CANCER
text:
This proposal seeks to enhance the potency of adoptive T cell immunotherapies and chimeric antigen receptor
T cells (CART) against cancer by removing a key inhibitory factor, CD5, from T-cells. The proposed research
is highly relevant to public health because CART immunotherapy, despite being now routine clinical practice,
still fails in a significant subset of patients. The project is relevant to those parts of the NCI’s mission that pertain
to the treatment of cancer, and the advancement of scientific knowledge and help all people live longer,
healthier lives.

title: Visualizing the hidden physical cues: Probing Live Cell Membrane Tension Dynamics in Health and Disease
text:
Project Title
Visualizing the hidden physical cues – Probing Live Cell Membrane Tension Dynamics in Health and Disease
Project Narrative
As cells naturally grow and develop in their niche environment, they experience physical forces and in response cue how
they spatiotemporally coordinate the mechanical work exerted around themselves to attain proper morphological changes,
rendering cell membrane tension key—both as a reporter and a regulator for critical dynamic processes such as mitosis,
embryogenesis, viral entry, liposome fusion, and apoptosis. To resolve membrane tension dynamics in live cells—and do
so in a quantitative, non-disruptive manner, and monitor continuously throughout the entire dynamic event, we innovate
existing biophysical methodologies and implement a two-pronged approach: extracellularly with membrane tether assay
using high-resolution optical tweezers, and intracellularly with genetically-encoded tension gauges by repurposing
mechanosensitive ion channels for robust image-based assays. The significance of our research program is that, with our
incisive experiments, we can connect previous studies from diverse modes of measurements to a unifying model, establish
membrane tension as quantitative mechanical biomarkers to characterize mechanistic details and differences between
healthy and disease state (e.g., metastatic cells are softer), and ultimately expand our understanding on how cells interpret
and integrate mechanical cues that shape their fate.

title: Title: Functional Annotation of Genomes via Phenotypic Convergence within Large Multi-species Alignments
text:
This research project will deliver innovative computational tools to identify genes and regulatory
elements responsible for specific organismal traits. These tools will enable researchers around
the world to assign functional elements to phenotypes of importance to human health and
disease, including longevity, neurological function, metabolism, and congenital diseases of
development. These genetic inferences will also provide new directions for the research
community to pursue a fundamental understanding of biological systems.

title: Identification of age-regulating breast cancer dormancy genes using C. elegans dauers
text:
The recurrence of breast cancer years after the initial disease was removed and treated remains a major cause
of patient mortality, yet we know little about the genes and pathways that control cancer cell dormancy and
reawakening. This proposal will exploit the similarities between the naturally occurring dormancy program in the
genetic model, C. elegans, and a 3D bone model of breast cancer dormancy to discover, validate and
characterize genes and regulatory pathways with conserved dormancy-regulating functions. Our proposed
studies will facilitate the discovery of targetable pathways that could enhance breast cancer patient survival by
suppressing disease recurrence.

title: Unleashing Natural Immunity Against Epstein-Barr Virus
text:
Unleashing Natural Immunity Against Epstein-Barr Virus
NARRATIVE
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 95% of the adult human population and is linked to serious diseases
like multiple sclerosis and cancer, yet no FDA-approved treatments exist. This research will elucidate how the
antiviral enzyme APOBEC3B restricts EBV infection and alters viral pathogenesis in vivo by disrupting its
inhibition by the viral ribonucleotide reductase (RNR). These studies have the potential to lead to an effective
therapeutic approach to cure symptomatic EBV infections and help prevent chronic EBV-associated diseases
including infectious mononucleosis and cancer, ultimately improving public health.

title: Generating Exogenic Organs for Transplantation without the Use of Immunosuppression
text:
This proposal is designed to utilize state-of-the-art gene editing technology for knocking out genes that control
liver development in the mouse embryo. To replace that liver with one derived from a rat, we will then inject stem
cells from a donor rat into the blastocyst of the mouse. This should allow the mouse fetus to grow and function
with a new liver that is derived from an entirely different animal species than mouse. These pilot studies are
designed to ultimately develop a reproducible and efficient method for generating human livers in pigs for
transplantation without the need for immunosuppression; and represent a glimpse into the future of highly
individualized medicine.

title: Mechanisms of spatiotemporal signaling by GPCRs
text:
The proposed research will contribute fundamental insights into how signaling through G protein-coupled
receptors (GPCRs) is organized and regulated in the cell. Because GPCRs control essentially every
physiological process, this new knowledge will be informative for the design of therapeutics to treat a wide range
of diseases.

title: Defining the role of linear and nonlinear forces in regulating cell metabolism
text:
Mechanotransduction is the process of converting mechanical forces from the external environment into
intracellular chemical signals. However, the complexity of the in vivo extracellular environment limits mechanistic
insight into how both linear and nonlinear mechanical properties regulate cellular metabolism. Understanding
this process will provide foundational knowledge in mechano-metabolic biology and enable the development of
tools for studying tissue development, in health and disease.

title: Computer-assisted diagnosis of ear pathologies by combining digital otoscopy with complementary data using machine learning
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because we are generating new methods aimed at
improving diagnostic quality and reducing interobserver variability, which will ultimately enable more
accurate diagnosis and personalized therapeutic approaches for ear abnormalities. Thus, the
proposed research is relevant to NIH’s mission pertaining to the application of novel strategies that
may improve human health and NIDCD’s mission of improving the diagnosis and treatment of ear
diseases, particularly otitis media.

title: Identifying and modulating pathologic T cells that govern oral mucosal immune related adverse events from immune checkpoint blockade
text:
Oral mucosal immune-related adverse events secondary to anti-PD-1 can cause serious morbidity and pain;
here, we seek to understand the pathogenesis of these oral mucosal adverse events. Here we propose an
innovative plan incorporating interrogation of human specimens, generation and analysis of novel mouse
models, and validation using patient-derived organoid cultures. This work is highly relevant to cancer patients'
oral health given the increasing use of immune stimulating systemic agents and the significant morbidity of these
oral mucosal side effects.

title: The role of platelets in the pathogenesis of alcohol-associated liver disease
text: Alcohol-associated liver disease is a pressing public health problem and accounts for increasing mortality due to cirrhosis in the United States. Effective and safe treatments for alcohol-associated liver disease are severely lacking. This project proposes a new paradigm of pathogenesis in alcohol-associated liver disease with the possibility for novel therapies.

title: Project 2: Analyses of the human GBM microenvironment form clinical trial specimens treated with the oncolytic HSV, rQNestin34v.2
text:
We are pursuing detailed immunologic, biologic, and imaging analyses on human GBMs that were treated in a
phase 1 clinical trial with a novel oncolytic virus (OV). We find that this form of immunotherapy induces a rapid
T cell response characterized by infiltration of treated GBMs with CD8+, CD4+ T cells and B cells. Both the
abundance of transcripts related to T cell and B cell infiltrates and the imaging changes observed correlate with
patient responses. Proposed further analyses of tumors and peripheral blood will characterize changes
associated with a response as well as characterize the tumor and viral antigens that these immune cells respond
to. These studies are needed to fully understand the results of this completed trial in order to inform avenues to
improve GBM immunotherapy.

title: Molecular mechanisms of load-induced t-tubule regulation in the mammalian heart
text: This proposal will determine how changing mechanical load, such as occurs when the heart has to pump against a high pressure, influences structures of the heart muscle membrane called transverse tubules. These (t)-tubules are disrupted in diseases such as heart failure, but how changing the load of the heart affects them is not known. Understanding this process, and the molecules responsible, might help in discovering new treatments for heart failure.

title: Project 1: Molecular Determinants of GIST Pathogenesis
text:
RP1: Molecular Determinants of GIST Pathogenesis
Narrative
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), a common subtype of soft tissue sarcoma, often exhibits aggressive
clinical behavior, and is incurable in advanced and metastatic settings. Through genomic and clinical analysis of
large cohorts of patients with GIST, we associated MAX/MGA/MYC genetic alterations and arm-level deletions
of 1p with metastatic GIST and poor relapse-free survival in resected GIST. Here, we propose comprehensive,
collaborative, and multidisciplinary studies to investigate the mechanisms of MAX/MGA/MYC perturbation
involved in aggressive GIST behavior, identify, and validate molecular biomarkers predictive of recurrence risk,
and develop a combinatorial pathologic-genomic nomogram to guide adjuvant imatinib therapy decisions and
identify novel strategies to target metastasis in advanced GIST.

title: Time-restricted feeding and breast cancer
text:
Aging and obesity are strong risk factors for breast cancer in women because as ovarian
estrogen declines, women have less protection from the harmful effects of obesity, which
causes inflammation and increases insulin levels. These harmful effects can be reversed
by weight loss but this is often not sustainable. We have shown that a novel dietary
intervention using time-restricted feeding of a western-style, high-fat diet prevents the
effect of obesity to drive breast cancer in mice; the proposed studies will investigate the
mechanisms underlying this beneficial effect.

title: Interrogation of bacterial pathogen canonical and non-canonical phosphorylation events
text:
A major goal in biology is to provide a complete and quantitative description of cellular behavior which includes
the analysis of canonical and non-canonical post-translational modifications as rapid switches of protein function.
Our continued development of phosphorylation SuperBinder reagents and associated methods address the
current inability to obtain comprehensive canonical and non-canonical phosphoproteomic profiles to understand
the dynamic landscape of phosphorylation switching upon external perturbations in eukaryotes and prokaryotes.

title: Mechanisms of p300 Activation During Pluripotency and Differentiation.
text:
The chromatin state at enhancers is well-defined, but it remains unknown how each feature of enhancer
chromatin contributes to overall enhancer activity. This proposal will determine novel principles regulating p300
activity during pluripotency and pre-implantation development. Understanding developmental enhancer
activation may provide insight into the pathogenesis of many diseases and syndromes in which enhancer
dysregulation has been implicated, including developmental syndromes and cancer.

title: Core E: Imaging
text: Core E: Imaging Project Summary The Imaging Core for the “Healthy Aging and Senile Dementia” study is responsible for all aspects of brain imaging performed in the Program Project Grant. This includes oversight of participant safety during imaging visits, clinical review of imaging for incidental findings, communication of imaging results, and quantitative post processing. The magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and amyloid and tau positron emission tomography (PET) protocols are compatible with CLARiTI and SCAN, which are two key harmonization initiatives across Alzheimer Disease Research Centers (ADRCs) in the US. A new element added with the grant renewal is post processing of tau PET using Siemen’s SyngoVia clinical product, which is FDA 510K cleared, and will allow for better translation of the results from the Biomarker Cohort to clinical populations. Similarly, we now provide a Centiloid value for all amyloid PET scans. Quantitative MRI, amyloid PET, and tau PET results will be provided to Core C: Data Management & Biostatistics in the form of data freezes for distribution to the Projects. When applicable, Core E: Imaging can also release images and reports back to the participant’s clinical team for the purpose of ongoing clinical care, following established HIPAA-compliant workflows.
